problem_statement: Extract the first three characters of a user's email before the @ symbol.

segments.heading: Let's slice a real string.
segments.sub: The problem: pull the first three characters of a user's email — the start of the username.
segments.narration: Let's put indexing to work on something real. Here's the task: given a user's email address, pull out the first three characters — the start of their username. We'll write the code, then walk through exactly what each part does.

segments.caption: Store the email in a variable.
segments.narration: First, we store the email in a variable called email. The string is alice, at example dot com. Think of it as a row of characters, each at a numbered position, starting from zero.

segments.caption: [0:3] means: start at 0, stop before 3.
segments.narration: Now the slice. email, square bracket, zero, colon, three. This says: start at index zero, and take characters up to — but not including — index three. So it grabs positions zero, one, and two: a, l, i. The result is the string a-l-i.

segments.caption: The end is exclusive — position 3 is left out.
segments.narration: Here's the part that trips people up. Why doesn't it include index three, the second i? Because in Python slicing, the end number is exclusive. The slice stops right before it. A handy trick: subtract start from end, three minus zero, and you get exactly three characters. Not four.

segments.caption: Negative indices count from the end — handy for suffixes.
segments.narration: Slicing works from the end too. email, bracket, minus three, colon, with nothing after the colon. Minus three starts three characters from the end, and the empty end means: go all the way to the last character. That pulls out c-o-m, the domain ending.

segments.caption: Edit the slice and run it. This is actual Python running in your browser.
segments.prompt: Now you try. Change the slice however you like and run it — this is real Python executing right here in the page. When you're done exploring, press Continue.
segments.narration: Now it's your turn, and this time it's real. The code below actually runs Python, right in your browser. Try changing the slice numbers — pull out the username, the domain, a single character, whatever you like. Run it, see the result, and press continue when you're ready.

config.starter_code:
email = 'alice@example.com'

# Try changing the slice:
username = email[0:3]
print(username)
config.hint: Try email[6:13] for the domain, or email[-3:] for 'com'.

segments.heading: What the slice taught us
recap_points: s[start:end] takes characters from start up to but not including end.
end − start = how many characters you get.
Leave a side blank to go to the beginning or end: s[-3:].
segments.narration: Let's lock in what the slice taught us. First: start colon end takes characters from the start position up to, but not including, the end. Second: end minus start tells you how many characters you get. And third: you can leave either side of the colon blank to run to the beginning or the end of the string. Next, you'll practice this yourself.
